title: JPMorgan Chase Q1 2025 Earnings Call Transcript

sections.prepared_remarks: JPMorgan reporting record Q1 net income of $13.4 billion, up 7 percent year over year. Revenue of $41.9 billion, up 5 percent. EPS $4.56 on record net income and strong capital generation. We returned $4.4 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks. Return on tangible common equity was 19.3 percent. Our Markets division had its best Q1 in six years, with FICC revenues up 15 percent on elevated volatility and rate volatility in particular. Investment Banking fees grew 32 percent, driven by a strong debt capital markets calendar and recovering M&A advisory. Consumer banking credit quality is normalizing after several years of historically low charge-offs. Our credit card net charge-off rates have risen roughly 50 basis points year-over-year but remain below pre-pandemic levels. We are actively preparing for a slower growth environment — our fortress balance sheet is maintained with a CET1 ratio of 15.5 percent, well above regulatory minimums. We continue to hire talent in AI and technology — we have over 3,000 AI and data scientists building applications across risk management, fraud detection, and client service.
sections.financial_highlights: Revenue $41.9 billion, net income $13.4 billion, EPS $4.56. Net interest income of $23.1 billion, down 2 percent year over year as deposit repricing benefits normalize. Non-interest income of $18.8 billion, up 14 percent, driven by Markets and IB strength. Efficiency ratio improved to 55 percent. We maintained strong capital with CET1 ratio 15.5 percent and a total capital ratio of 17.8 percent. Tangible book value per share grew 11 percent year over year. Loan loss reserves increased by $900 million, primarily from card and commercial real estate. Our commercial real estate portfolio totalled $91 billion — primarily in office, where we are conservatively underwritten with average LTVs below 55 percent. We expect NII to be roughly flat in Q2 versus Q1, with further guidance to follow.
sections.qanda_session:
Matt Holler: Jamie, on credit — you're building reserves in cards but NCOs are still below pre-pandemic. How do you think about the normalization path? Are you expecting a soft landing or does the tariff environment introduce new uncertainty in the card portfolio?

Jamie Dimon: Matt, we are cautiously optimistic. Consumer balance sheets are generally strong but there are cracks forming at the lower income end. Card NCOs have stabilized at higher levels — we're not seeing dramatic further deterioration. The tariff situation adds macroeconomic uncertainty which could slow consumer spending. Our base case is a soft landing with rates gradually declining, but we prepare for adverse scenarios. On C&I lending, we are seeing companies pull back on capital expenditure plans due to policy uncertainty. That could reduce loan growth. We are actively stress-testing our portfolio against a scenario where inflation persists and rates remain elevated longer. Our credit risk models are updated monthly. We also use our AI-driven credit models extensively now — they are materially more predictive than our legacy statistical models, particularly for early-stage delinquency identification.

Ebrahim Poonawala: Jeremy, on the net interest income guide — can you help us size the deposit repricing tailwind and headwind as rates decline? And what's your expectation for deposit beta as the Fed cuts?

Jeremy Barnum: Ebrahim, on deposit repricing: as rates fall we're a net beneficiary because our deposit beta is relatively low. We have about $350 billion in interest-bearing deposits that will reprice upward in a rising rate environment and reprice downward more slowly. If rates fall 100 basis points, we estimate our NII benefit from deposit repricing lags is roughly $1.2 billion annually. The challenge is that falling rates also compress asset margins. Net-net, we are roughly NII neutral to slightly positive in a 100-bps rate cut scenario over 12 months. Our deposit franchise is sticky — our Chase app has 58 million users, and the switching cost for consumers is high. That gives us durable deposit pricing power.
sections.forward_outlook: Jamie Dimon: I'll be direct: I still believe there are significant economic risks ahead — the fiscal deficit is historically high, geopolitical tensions are elevated, and there is a real chance of stagflation. If I am wrong and it's a soft landing, this business will perform exceptionally. If I'm right about the risks, our fortress balance sheet positions us to take advantage of dislocations, just as we did in 2008. We have built a company that can navigate from either direction. The investment in technology — $14 billion annually — is increasing our competitive moat. Our transaction banking platform is the best in the world. Our private bank handles $700 billion in AUM. Chase UK is profitable ahead of schedule. We will continue to invest in our people and our capabilities. A JPMorgan franchise that has a global network spanning consumer, wholesale, markets, asset management, and private banking is extraordinarily resilient.
